subject: chemistry_2
question_text: What is relative lowering of vapour pressure? How is it useful to determine the molar mass of a solute?

verification.note: Unit 2 (Solutions) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.65-68, which prints the question and a model answer. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. The printed derivation (book p.66, SAQ 1) was checked line by line and its algebra is sound: from (p⁰ − pₛ)/p⁰ = n₂/n₁ with n₂ = w₂/M₂ and n₁ = w₁/M₁, rearranging gives M₂ = w₂M₁p⁰ / (w₁(p⁰ − pₛ)), which is what the book prints. BOOK GAP: the book writes "For dilute solutions n₂ << n₁, hence n₂ can be neglected in the denominator" without saying that this is an APPROXIMATION and that the exact form keeps n₂ there. That is stated on this card, because the same approximation is what makes SAQ 4 of this unit answer 8 g rather than 10 g. BOOK TYPO: the printed line ii) has "vapour PRESSURE" in capitals mid-sentence, a scanner artifact; it is written normally here. The book also mixes ω and w for the masses in the same derivation; w is used throughout here.

steps.label: Relative lowering of vapour pressure
lines: When a non-volatile solute is dissolved in
a solvent, the vapour pressure of the
solution pₛ is lower than the vapour
pressure of the pure solvent p⁰.
The lowering of vapour pressure is
(p⁰ − pₛ).
The ratio of this lowering to the vapour
pressure of the pure solvent is called the
relative lowering of vapour pressure.
steps.why: The lowering on its own depends on which solvent is used, because a solvent with a high vapour pressure gives a large lowering for the same solute. Dividing by p⁰ removes that dependence and leaves a pure number, which is why the RELATIVE lowering, and not the lowering, is the quantity Raoult's law states.
common_mistakes: Defining it as (p⁰ − pₛ) alone. Without dividing by p⁰ it is the lowering, not the relative lowering.
Writing pₛ − p⁰. The solution has the lower vapour pressure, so the pure solvent value comes first.
steps.memory_tip: Lowering divided by the pure solvent value. The word relative means divided by p⁰.
steps.margin_note: Define the two symbols p⁰ and pₛ as you write them. This mark is for the definition plus its ratio.

steps.label: Raoult's law form
lines: By Raoult's law, for a dilute solution of a
non-volatile solute, the relative lowering
is equal to the mole fraction of the
solute:
n₁ = moles of solvent
n₂ = moles of solute
steps.why: A non-volatile solute adds nothing to the vapour, so the vapour pressure of the solution is only the solvent's share, pₛ = p⁰x₁. Subtracting from p⁰ and using x₁ + x₂ = 1 leaves the relative lowering equal to x₂. This one line is what connects a measurable pressure to a count of solute particles.
common_mistakes: Equating the relative lowering to x₁, the mole fraction of the solvent. It equals the mole fraction of the SOLUTE.
Leaving out the words "non-volatile". A volatile solute has its own vapour pressure and the relation does not hold.
steps.memory_tip: Relative lowering equals the mole fraction of the solute. Everything after this is algebra.
steps.margin_note: This is the marked line of the whole derivation. Write it on its own line and name the law beside it.

steps.label: The dilute solution step
lines: For a dilute solution n₂ is much smaller
than n₁, so n₂ may be left out of the
denominator:
Writing each number of moles as mass
divided by molar mass,

lines.text: n₂ = w₂ / M₂ and n₁ = w₁ / M₁

steps.why: The exact relation has n₁ + n₂ in the denominator, so the unknown M₂ appears twice on the right-hand side. Dropping n₂ is an approximation, valid only while the solution is dilute, and it is what leaves the short form written in the next step. Say that it is an approximation: the same step is why SAQ 4 of this unit answers 8 g instead of the exact 10 g.
common_mistakes: Dropping n₂ from the NUMERATOR as well. Only the n₂ in the denominator is neglected; the solute is the whole point of the numerator.
Turning the moles upside down. n = mass / molar mass, so w₂/M₂ goes on top and w₁/M₁ below.
steps.memory_tip: Dilute means n₂ is small next to n₁, so only the denominator loses it.
steps.margin_note: Write the words "for a dilute solution" before this step. Without them the line is not correct and the mark is at risk.

steps.label: The molar mass formula
lines: Rearranging for the molar mass of the
solute M₂:
w₂ = mass of solute, w₁ = mass of solvent
M₁ = molar mass of the solvent
So by weighing w₁ and w₂ and measuring p⁰
and pₛ, the molar mass of the solute is
found.
steps.why: Every quantity on the right is measurable: two masses on a balance and two vapour pressures on a manometer. That is the whole use of the relative lowering — it is a colligative property, so it counts solute particles, and a count of particles together with a known mass gives the mass of one mole.
common_mistakes: Putting M₁ in the denominator. The molar mass of the SOLVENT multiplies on top; the mass of the solvent w₁ is below.
Answering only the first half of the question. The question asks two things, so the formula for M₂ must be reached, not just defined.
steps.memory_tip: Solute mass, solvent molar mass and p⁰ on top; solvent mass and the lowering (p⁰ − pₛ) below.
steps.margin_note: Box the formula and list every symbol under it. The symbol list is what shows the formula was derived and not recalled.

insider_note: The question has two halves and the second one carries most of the marks. A script that defines relative lowering beautifully and never reaches M₂ = w₂M₁p⁰ / (w₁(p⁰ − pₛ)) is a half answer.
